summary: Explains the difference between information models and data models for defining managed objects in network management. It analyzes how specifications from the IETF and bodies such as the ITU and DMTF fit into each category, to reduce ongoing confusion about the terms.

eli5.summary: One kind of model is a sketch of what things mean, like an idea drawing. The other is the detailed blueprint for building it. This note explains which is which.

questions: difference between information and data models
what is a data model in network management
subtitle: Why a conceptual information model and an implementation-level data model are different things, with examples from IETF, ITU and DMTF.

tldr.problem: People used the terms Information Model and Data Model differently, which caused confusion and long arguments about languages for defining managed objects.
tldr.mechanism: The note, from an IRTF NMRG workshop, defines an information model as a conceptual, protocol-neutral model and a data model as a detailed, protocol-specific one, and sorts MIBs, PIBs, CIM schemas and others accordingly.
tldr.outcome: One information model can lead to several data models, though there is a gray area between the two.

facts.label: IM to DM
facts.value: One IM can yield multiple DMs

today: RFC 3444 is an Informational RFC and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It remains a terminology reference for the difference between information models and data models.

sections.title: Why the Terms Needed Defining
sections.content:
Several languages exist for defining managed objects, such as the Structure of Management Information (SMI), the Structure of Policy Provisioning Information (SPPI) and the DMTF's Managed Object Format (MOF). Discussions about their merits, including an IETF BoF on Network Information Modeling in August 2000, showed that people understood "Information Model" (IM) and "Data Model" (DM) differently.

The IRTF Network Management Research Group (NMRG) dedicated its 8th workshop (Austin, December 2000) to harmonizing the terms, with experts from the IETF, DMTF and ITU. This document presents the outcome and, unlike short definitions elsewhere such as RFC 3198, explains the rationale and gives examples.
sections.eli5: People kept using two words to mean different things and arguing. So a group got together to agree on what each word means.

sections.title: Two Models for Two Purposes
sections.content:
The key observation is that IMs and DMs differ because they serve different purposes. An information model models managed objects at a conceptual level, independent of any specific implementation or transport protocol. It should hide protocol and implementation details, and it defines relationships between managed objects.

A data model sits at a lower level of abstraction, is intended for implementors and includes protocol-specific constructs. Since a conceptual model can be implemented in different ways, multiple DMs can be derived from a single IM.

The line is not always sharp. There is a gray area where the two overlap, like the gray areas between analysis, high-level design and low-level design models in object-oriented software engineering.
sections.eli5: An information model is the idea drawing of a treehouse. A data model is the exact plan with every nail. One idea drawing can lead to many plans.

sections.title: Information Models
sections.content:
IMs help designers describe the managed environment, help operators understand the modeled objects, and guide implementors on what the DMs must describe. They are protocol neutral and can generally and should specify relationships between objects.

An IM can be informal, in natural language. An example is RFC 3290, a conceptual model of a Diffserv router. Within the IETF it is exceptional for an IM to be explicit, and more so for the IM and DM to be in separate RFCs. Then the IM is usually Informational and the DM usually Standards Track. Most RFCs defining an SNMP MIB module include some informal description of the model behind it, as RFC 2863 does for the Interfaces Group MIB, but most are rudimentary and incomplete.

IMs can also be formal or semi-formal, for example with UML class diagrams, which the DMTF, ITU-T SG 4, 3GPP SA5, the TeleManagement Forum and the ATM Forum routinely use. The note advises object-oriented techniques, especially abstraction, encapsulation and methods.
sections.eli5: Information models can be written in plain words or drawn as boxes and arrows. Both show what things exist and how they connect.

sections.title: Data Models and Where Real Specifications Fall
sections.content:
DMs define managed objects with implementation and protocol details, such as rules for mapping objects onto lower-level protocol constructs. Most management models standardized so far are DMs:

  • IETF MIB modules, written in SMI (derived from ASN.1).
  • IETF PIB modules, written in SPPI (close to SMI, also derived from ASN.1).
  • OSI MIB modules from ISO, now maintained by the ITU-T, written in GDMO.
  • DMTF CIM Schemas, with a non-normative graphical UML form and a normative textual form in MOF.

IETF MIB modules include details such as OID assignments, indexing structures, MAX-ACCESS and STATUS clauses and conformance statements. Because CIM Schemas have a graphical notation, one could argue they are closer to IMs than IETF MIB modules.

SMIng, a language defined by the NMRG, was designed at a higher conceptual level and can map onto SNMP and COPS-PR, so it is more protocol neutral. It is still a DM, since UML and ER diagrams express relationships better. The IETF SMING Working Group chose instead to develop SMIv3, aimed primarily at SNMP.
sections.eli5: Data models are the detailed rule books each group wrote for its own system. Some come with pictures, some do not, but all of them have the nitty-gritty details.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The note states that the meaning of the terms Information Model and Data Model has no direct security impact on the Internet. It is a terminology document and defines no protocol.
sections.eli5: Agreeing on what two words mean does not make the internet any less safe.
